sentences.text: JUDGMENT
The appellant/complainant feeling aggrieved by the judgment of Trial Court on the file of Principal Civil Judge and JMFC, Hassan in C.C.No.2791/2017, dated 29.12.2018, preferred this appeal.
2. Parties to the appeal are referred with their ranks as assigned in the Trial Court for the sake of convenience.
3. Heard the argument of both sides.

4. On careful perusal of oral and documentary evidence placed on record, it would go to show that accused has borrowed a sum of Rs.5,00,000/- on 25.10.2016 for family exigencies and to purchase a site.
Accused, in order to discharge the said lawful debt, issued cheque bearing No.288065, dated 30.03.2017 drawn on Punjab National Bank, Hassan, Ex.P.1.
Complainant presented the said cheque through his banker Hassan Branch and the same was dishonoured for want of sufficient funds in the account of accused vide bank endorsement Ex.

P.2. 
NC: 2023:KHC:29434 Thereafter, demand notice was issued on 12.04.2017 Ex.P.3 and postal receipt is produced at Ex.P.4.
The demand notice sent through registered post was refused by accused on 13.04.2017.
Accused has not paid the amount covered under cheque Ex.P.1 and complaint is filed on 05.05.2017.

If the above referred documents and evidence of PW.1 are appreciated, then it is evident that complainant has complied the legal requirement in terms of Section 138 and 142 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (for short 'N.I.Act').

When issuance of cheque with signature of accused on the account maintained by accused is admitted or proved, then necessary statutory presumption will have to be drawn in terms of Section 118 and 139 of N.I. Act.
5.

In this context of the matter, it is useful to refer the judgment of Hon'ble Apex Court in APS Forex Services Pvt. Ltd. Vs. Shakti International Fashion Linkers and others reported in AIR 2020 SC 945,
wherein it has been observed and held that once the issuance and NC: 2023:KHC:29434 signature on cheque is admitted, there is always a presumption in favour of complainant that there exist legally enforceable debt or liability.

entities.text: APS Forex Services Pvt. Ltd. Vs. Shakti International Fashion Linkers and others reported in AIR 2020 SC 945
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Plea by accused that cheque was given by way of security and same has been misused by complainant is not tenable.
6. It also profitable to refer another judgment of Hon'ble Apex Court in P. Rasiya vs. Abdul Nazer and another reported in 2022 SCC OnLine SC 1131, wherein it has been observed and held that'

entities.text: P. Rasiya vs. Abdul Nazer and another reported in 2022 SCC OnLine SC 1131
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: "Once the initial burden is discharged by the complainant that the cheque was issued by the accused and signature of accused on the cheque is not disputed, then in that case, the onus will shift upon the accused to prove the contrary that the cheque was not for discharge of any debt or other liability.

The presumption under Section 139 of N.I. Act is statutory presumption and thereafter, once it is Yogesh T R vs Smt. Nandhini on 18 August, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/124070990/
2 presumed that the cheque is issued in whole or in part of any debt or other liability which is in favour of the complainant/holder of the cheque, NC: 2023:KHC:29434 in that case it is for the accused to prove the contrary."

sentences.text: In view of principles enunciated in both these decisions, if the evidence of PW.1 and the documents are appreciated then it would go to show that complainant has discharged his initial burden of proving that cheque in question Ex.P.1 was issued for lawful discharge of debt.
7. It is now up to accused to place rebuttal evidence to displace the initial presumption available in favour of the complainant under Sections 118 and 139 of N.I. Act.
Accused apart from the relevant material brought on record in the cross-examination of PW.1, also relies on the evidence of DW.1 and the document at Ex.D.1.
Whether the said rebuttal evidence placed on record by accused is sufficient to displace the statutory presumption in favour of the complainant or not has to be decided.

The Trial Court has recorded finding that complainant has no money lending license for running Sri Dhanalaxmi Finance and Investments, on which the cheque has been drawn as per Ex.P.1,
secondly, there is inconsistent evidence of money being given to accused and lastly, signature on cheque is not that of accused.
9.

The description of complainant in the complaint and evidence of PW.1 would go to show that complainant is the Proprietor of Sri Dhanalaxmi Finance and Investments and accused has borrowed money of Rs.5,00,000/- for family exigencies and to purchase a house site on 25.10.2016.
However, complainant in the complaint averments does not specifically plead that accused availed loan from Sri Dhanalaxmi Finance and Investments.

However, the evidence of PW.1 and the admitted issuance of cheque Ex.P.1 would go to show that money was borrowed from Sri Dhanalaxmi Finance and Investments and to discharge the said debt, cheque under Ex.P.1 has been issued.
Learned counsel for the appellant has filed I.A.No.2/2019 under Section 391 of Cr.P.C. and produced copy of money lending license.
11. Learned counsel for the respondent submitted that same be considered at the time of final disposal of this appeal.

When issuance of cheque in the name of complainant representing Sri Dhanalaxmi Finance and Investments is proved, then if the document of money lending license produced under I.A.No.2/2019 is taken on record then no any serious prejudice would be caused to accused.
Learned counsel for the respondent also submits that other grounds are required to be decided.
Accordingly, I.A.No.2/2019 is disposed of.

In view of the submissions of learned counsel for the respondent, finding of Trial Court that complainant was not having any money lending license as on the date of transaction cannot be legally sustained.

sentences.text: The second contention of learned counsel for the respondent is that there is inconsistent evidence as to NC: 2023:KHC:29434 where money was actually paid.
The complaint averments speaks to the effect that money was paid in the office of complainant.

The evidence of PW.1 would go to show that PW.1 at one breath has stated that accused has received the money in the office and at another breath has stated that accused has taken money from his house.
The mere said inconsistent evidence of PW.1 as to where money was paid cannot by itself said as sufficient evidence to hold that no money has been paid by the complainant to the accused.

13. It is the contention of accused that she has no any transaction with the complainant and her husband may be having financial transaction with the complainant and in support of such contention, Ex.D.1 judgment in O.S.No.26/2016 is produced.

On perusal of the evidence of DW.1 and Ex.D.1, it would go to show that defendant No.2 H.C.Shivakumar is the husband of accused and complainant had filed the suit against Ravi and husband of complainant for the relief of specific performance.
In the NC: 2023:KHC:29434 said suit, defendant No.2 is the brother of defendant No.1 was not in dispute and the suit came to be decreed.
The transaction involved in Ex.D.1 and the one covered under Ex.P.1 has no any nexus at all, so as to disbelieve the evidence of PW.1 that accused has not borrowed any money from the complainant.
The transaction covered under Ex.D.1 is dated 24.02.2014, whereas the cheque in question is dated 30.03.2017.
The accused by way of defence evidence of DW.1 did not establish any nexus between the two transactions.
Therefore, the evidence of DW.1 and Ex.D.1 cannot be accepted as sufficient rebuttal evidence to disprove the evidence of PW.1 to the effect that Ex.P.1 was issued for lawful discharge of debt.
14. The accused has also made feeble attempt in her evidence that demand notice as per Ex.P.3 is not duly served to the accused.
The demand notice issued to accused by registered post Ex.P.5 returned as "refused" on 13.04.2017.
The registered post was sent on the correct address of accused as shown in the cause-title on the very - 10 - NC: 2023:KHC:29434 same address.
The Trial Court being satisfied with the proper service of notice has issued NBW against accused.
On 06.01.2018, accused appeared through counsel and was released on bail.
Accused at the first available opportunity did not choose to complain that the address shown in the cause-title of the complaint is not correct and demand notice is not served on her.

It is pertinent to note that when the accused has chosen to contest the claim of complainant, he never made any written communication expressing her defence in challenging the correctness of the address shown in the complaint, so as to make basic foundation to deny service of demand notice as per Ex.P.3.
15.

In this context of the matter, it is profitable to refer the Judgment of Hon'ble Apex Court in C.C.Alavi Haji vs. Palapetty Muhammed and another reported in (2007) 6 SCC 555, wherein it has been served and held that :-
"

sentences.text:
It is not necessary to aver in the complaint under Section 138 of the N.I.Act that service of notice was evaded by the accused or Yogesh T R vs Smt. Nandhini on 18 August, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/124070990/
4 - 11 - NC: 2023:KHC:29434 that the accused had a role to play in the return of the notice unserved.

entities.text: Yogesh T R vs Smt. Nandhini
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: When Section 114 of the Evidence Act, 1872 is applied to communications sent by post, it enables the Court to presume that in the common course of natural events, the communication would have been delivered at the address of the addressee.
But the presumption that is raised under Section 27 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 is a far stronger presumption.
While 114 of the Evidence Act refers to a general presumption, Section 27 of 1897 Act refers to a specific presumption.
Section 27 of the 1897 Act gives raise to a presumption that service of notice has been effected when it is sent to the correct address by registered post.

In view of the said presumption when stating that a notice has been sent by registered post to the address of the drawer, it is unnecessary to further aver in the complaint that inspite of the return of the notice unserved, it is deemed to have been served or that the addressee is deemed to have knowledge of the notice.

Unless and until the contrary is proved by the addressee, service of notice is deemed to have been effected at the - 12 - NC: 2023:KHC:29434 time at which the letter would have been delivered in the ordinary course of business.

The Supreme court has already held that when a notice is sent by registered post and is returned with a postal endorsement "refused" or "not available in the house" or "house locked" or "
shop closed" or " addressee is not in station", due service has to be presumed."

Therefore, in view of the principles enunciated in the aforementioned judgment and the above referred evidence on record, it cannot be contended that there is no proper service of demand notice on the accused.
16. The last contention of accused is that, signature appearing on Ex.P.1 is not that of accused.
Learned counsel for respondent has argued that the name of accused is "Nandita" and she has signed as "Nandita" only and never signed as "Nandhini".
Therefore, the contention of complainant that accused has issued cheque for lawful discharge of debt cannot be accepted.
On careful perusal of cause-title shown in the complaint, accused is described as "Nandhini" w/o Shivakumar.
Accused has not disputed that she is the wife of Shivakumar against whom the complainant had filed suit in O.S.No.26/2016 seeking specific performance of contract.

Accused has signed as "Nandita" on the statement recorded under Section 313 Cr.P.C., wherein the plea that has been recorded orally and has signed as "Nandita" in the order sheet dated 06.01.2018 and also in the vakalat filed before Trial Court signed as "Nandita", whereas accused has signed as "Nandhini" in the cheque issued to complainant Ex.P.1.
It is pertinent to note that the very same accused, in this appeal, while appearing through counsel signed on the vakalat as "Nandhini" as signed in Ex.P.1.

Therefore, it is evident that accused has deliberately changed her signature in the Court proceedings Yogesh T R vs Smt. Nandhini on 18 August, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/124070990/
5 as "Nandita" though she has signed as "Nandhini" in Ex.P.1 and on the vakalat filed in this appeal.

entities.text: Yogesh T R vs Smt. Nandhini
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It is pertinent to note that bank has not dishonoured the cheque of accused on the ground that signature differs at Return Reason Code No.12 vide endorsement Ex.P.2. Accused has not examined the Bank Manager to show that her specimen signature provided to the Bank is not the one as appeared in Ex.P.1.

Therefore, it will have to be held that accused only with an intention to defeat the claim of complainant for the amount covered under the cheque Ex.P.1 made attempts to sign as "Nandita" in the Court proceedings, as against the one appearing on the Cheque Ex.P.1 is not that of accused cannot be legally sustained.

19. When the accused has failed to probabilise his defence by way of rebuttal evidence to displace the statutory presumption available in favour of complainant, then necessary presumption will have to be drawn in terms of Section 118 and 139 of N.I.Act that Cheque in Ex.P.1 was issued for lawful discharge of debt.

The Trial Court without properly appreciating the evidence on record - 15 - NC: 2023:KHC:29434 has arrived at an improper conclusion holding that cheque Ex.P.1 was not issued for lawful discharge of debt.

The complainant has proved by evidence on record that accused has committed offence under Section 138 of N.I. Act.
20.
Now coming to the question of imposition of sentence.
The Court will have to impose appropriate sentence looking to the facts and circumstances of the case, nature of evidence brought on record and other attending circumstances.

If the said factors are considered and appreciated with reference to the case at hand, then, if accused is sentenced to pay a fine of Rs.5,10,000/- in default of payment of fine, to undergo simple imprisonment for six months is ordered, will meet the ends of justice.

Consequently, proceed to pass the following:-
Order
Appeal filed by the appellant/complainant is hereby allowed.
The judgment of Trial Court on the file of Principal Civil Judge and JMFC, Hassan in C.C.No.2791/2017, dated 29.12.2018 is hereby set aside.
The accused is sentenced to pay fine of Rs.5,10,000/-, in default of payment of fine, shall undergo simple imprisonment for six months.

In view of exercising power under Section 357(3) of Cr.P.C., out of the fine amount as ordered above, Rs.5,00,000/- is ordered to be given to the complainant as compensation and remaining Yogesh T R vs Smt. Nandhini on 18 August, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/124070990/
